segments.name: Pithiviers and the Trades That Failed

stops.name: Pithiviers, the birth in the Gâtinais
stops.date_confidence: attested for 21 June 1781 by MacTutor and en.wikipedia, following Arago's near-contemporary notice; a later secondary source gives 27 June and the two figures conflict, recorded here and not resolved. The birth house is unlocated, so the marker sits on the Pithiviers town centre at 48.1728, 2.2525; the research pool's geography lens gave 48.1801, 2.2526, which falls about 800 m north in open country, and that value is corrected rather than inherited.
stops.campa: In the small town of Pithiviers, in the Orléanais country that will be redrawn as the Loiret, a son is born to Siméon Poisson, a soldier who came home from the army with no advancement and took what the town would give him: a clerk's place, then a seat among its administrators. The Revolution is eight years off. When it comes it will carry the father up to the presidency of the district, and the boy will grow up watching a man of no birth handed authority by a change in the law. The house itself is not identified in anything that survives.
suggested_refs: The parish and civil registers of Pithiviers, Loiret, for June 1781
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Siméon-Denis Poisson

stops.name: Outside Pithiviers, the nail and the swaddling bands
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The anecdote traces to François Arago's 1850 eulogy of Poisson before the Académie des sciences and reaches this file at one remove, through later biographical summaries; it is family tradition, not a document. The date orders the segment and should not be quoted: only the infancy is indicated. The nurse's house is unrecovered, so the coordinate marks the Pithiviers countryside and nothing narrower.
stops.campa: His mother's health is poor, so the infant goes out to a wet nurse in the country, as half the children of France do. The story the family keeps, and Arago repeats over his coffin sixty-nine years later, is that the father arrives one day to find the nurse gone out and the child slung from a nail in the wall by his swaddling bands, hung up out of reach of the animals. Arago tells it as a proof of election. No document stands behind it. The nurse is not named, her house is not recovered, and the only witness is a father telling his son about it afterwards.
suggested_refs: François Arago, éloge of Poisson read to the Académie des sciences, 1850
sources: Arago's 1850 notice as reflected in later mathematical biographies
MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Siméon-Denis Poisson

stops.name: Fontainebleau, the uncle's surgery
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor that his father sent him to an uncle, a surgeon at Fontainebleau, and that the apprenticeship failed, with poor manual coordination given as the reason. No year is fixed in the sources reached; 1793 orders the segment ahead of the documented 1796 return and should not be quoted as a date. A harsher variant in which a patient he bled died is unverified lore and is not carried.
stops.campa: The father wants his son inside a trade that cannot be taken away, and sends him to Fontainebleau to an uncle who is a surgeon. The instruments do not obey him. He cannot hold a line when he draws and cannot manage a lancet, and the uncle gives him up and sends him back to Pithiviers, to a father who had wanted him fixed in a profession. He is twelve or thirteen; no account of his life fixes the year, though every one of them tells the story. The house he goes back to has already worked out that he will have to earn.
suggested_refs: The surgical practice of Poisson's uncle at Fontainebleau, unidentified in the reachable record
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Siméon-Denis Poisson

stops.name: Fontainebleau, the École centrale and the problems on the desk
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests the enrolment: 'In 1796 Poisson was sent back to Fontainebleau by his father, this time to enrol in the École Centrale there.' MacTutor does not name Vanneau or Billy; those names, and the teacher studying ahead of his own pupil, trace only to Arago's 1850 eulogy and are [R]. The La Fontaine pun is reported by fr.wikipedia as a schoolroom tradition and is [R]. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: Sent back to Fontainebleau, this time to the new École centrale, he is shown a set of mathematical problems by a schoolfellow and solves them. The teacher Billy, in the account Arago gives, takes to studying ahead of his own pupil in order to stay in front of him, and gives up teaching him anything except the road to Paris. The boy who could not hold a lancet turns out to be able to hold an equation in his head entire. His schoolmaster puts the whole thing as a joke on the name.
stops.quote: Petit poisson deviendra grand, / Pourvu que Dieu lui prête vie.
stops.quote_source: Jean de La Fontaine, 'Le Petit Poisson et le Pêcheur', reported by fr.wikipedia as the pun his schoolmaster Billy made on the boy's surname; a tradition, not a documented utterance

stops.date_confidence: attested for 1798 by MacTutor and en.wikipedia, which report entry to the École Polytechnique and say he is reported to have placed first in the competitive entrance examination; the placing is reported rather than documented and is carried as such. The collection said to have been taken up by classmates is [R], with no subscriber list and no sum recovered. Month not recorded. stops.campa: He comes up to Paris at seventeen and is placed first in the entrance examination of a school three years old, founded to make engineers for a republic at war. He has almost no money. The story his classmates tell afterwards is of a collection taken up among them so the poor one from the Loiret could stay; no list of subscribers and no sum survives. Lagrange and Laplace are both teaching in the building that year, and the entering class is a few hundred boys chosen by competition out of the whole of France.

stops.name: École Polytechnique, the memoir Legendre sends on
stops.date_confidence: MacTutor attests that a memoir written at about eighteen, on the number of complete integrals of a finite-difference equation, attracted Legendre's attention, and that Poisson finished in 1800 without the usual final examination and was made répétiteur in analysis on Laplace's recommendation. MacTutor names Legendre alone; the addition of Lacroix as co-recommender and of the Recueil des savants étrangers as the place of publication comes from Arago's notice and is separated out here as [R]. An earlier memoir of 1799 on Bézout's method of elimination is [R], reported without a document. Month not recorded.
stops.campa: At eighteen he writes on the number of complete integrals a finite-difference equation can have. Legendre reads it and sends it forward; Arago's account puts Lacroix beside him and names the Recueil des savants étrangers as where it appeared. The school lets him finish in 1800 without sitting the final examination, on the strength of the paper, and then keeps him instead of sending him out to a corps. He is made répétiteur in analysis on Laplace's word, twenty years old, drilling the class he has just left.
suggested_refs: Poisson's memoir on the number of complete integrals of finite-difference equations, c. 1799-1800
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Siméon-Denis Poisson

stops.name: École Polytechnique, deputy professor at twenty-one
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1802 by MacTutor and en.wikipedia, both giving the appointment as substitute or deputy professor without a month. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json.
stops.campa: Two years as répétiteur and he is made deputy professor, a rank that puts him in front of the amphitheatre in his own right. He is twenty-one and has never worked anywhere else. He will never hold an engineering post, never go out to a province with a theodolite, never survey a coast. Everything he does he will do inside three or four buildings on the left bank and one across the river, and he starts here the habit his colleagues describe after his death: one problem at a time, carried to the end before the next is opened.

stops.name: École Polytechnique, the chair Fourier leaves
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia: Poisson took the chair of mechanics at the École Polytechnique in 1806, the chair vacated when Joseph Fourier went to Grenoble as prefect. Month not recorded. Arago's recollection of lodging next to Poisson is undated in his autobiography and Arago entered the school in 1803, so the passage belongs to these years but cannot be fixed to one of them. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json.
stops.campa: Joseph Fourier is sent to Grenoble to be a prefect, and his chair of mechanics falls to Poisson at twenty-four. He lectures fast, publishes without a pause, and works from Laplace's picture of matter: bodies made of molecules pulling on one another at short range, and everything observable to be got out of that by analysis alone. A younger man lodging next door, François Arago, comes into his room most evenings and stays for hours, arguing politics and mathematics.
stops.quote: It was there that I had the pleasure of making Poisson's acquaintance, who lived next to us. Every evening the great geometer entered my room, and we passed entire hours in conversing on politics and mathematics, which is certainly not quite the same thing.
stops.quote_source: François Arago, 'The History of My Youth', in Biographies of Distinguished Scientific Men (London and Boston, 1857); the French original appears in Oeuvres de François Arago
suggested_refs: Arago, 'Histoire de ma jeunesse', on the Polytechnique lodgings

stops.name: Arcueil, the Sunday society
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia 'Société d'Arcueil' dates the society 1806-1822 and names Poisson among the Sunday men with Biot, Malus, Thénard, Gay-Lussac, Arago and Humboldt. Month not recorded. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from pierre_simon_laplace.journey.json and augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json (48.7994, 2.3336); those files record that the pin sits roughly 800 m from the commune centre at 48.8075, 2.3361, and the discrepancy is inherited with the pin rather than re-derived.
stops.campa: South of Paris, on the Bièvre, Laplace has bought the house next to Berthollet's, and on Sundays the young men come out from the city to the two gardens: Biot, Malus, Thénard, Gay-Lussac, Arago, Alexander von Humboldt lately back from the Americas, and Poisson. There is no charter and no budget. Two old men decide between them which papers get read at the Institute, and the deciding is done in advance, at a table in a garden. Poisson is twenty-five. The society keeps meeting until 1822.
suggested_refs: Mémoires de physique et de chimie de la Société d'Arcueil (1807-1817)

stops.name: Paris, the theory of heat printed under one letter
stops.date_confidence: [R]. That Poisson published in the Bulletin de la Société Philomatique, over the signature 'P', the first printed account of Fourier's theory of heat propagation in solid bodies is carried by the research dossier and corroborated only in outline by MacTutor's account of his Academy and Bureau activity in these years; the Bulletin issue was not opened in this pass. Month not recorded. The Société Philomatique's own meeting place is not established here; the coordinate is the Institut de France pin, inherited byte-identical from evariste_galois.journey.json, itself from joseph_fourier.journey.json.
stops.campa: Fourier's memoir on the propagation of heat has been read to the Institute and refused publication; Lagrange and Laplace will not accept the trigonometric series. Then a summary of that theory appears in the Bulletin de la Société Philomatique, signed with the single letter P. Poisson has put Fourier's heat into print before Fourier could, in a journal he edits, under an initial. He then goes at the same problem down his own road, molecules and central forces, and comes out with answers that are not the same.
suggested_refs: Bulletin de la Société Philomatique de Paris, 1808, the notice signed 'P'
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Siméon-Denis Poisson

stops.date_confidence: attested for 1808 by MacTutor and en.wikipedia: attached to the Bureau des longitudes as an astronomer. No month recorded. The Bureau's own premises in this period were not pinned down by the research pool; the Observatory, over which the Bureau held authority, is the best-attested associated site. Coordinate 48.8368, 2.3364 inherited byte-identical from augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json in preference to the pool's 48.8377, 2.3364.
stops.campa: He is attached to the Bureau des longitudes as an astronomer, which in France means a seat on the small body that runs the calendar, the tables, the sea charts and the Observatory itself. He is not an observer and does not become one. What the post gives him is a second salary and a second room in which the state's mathematics is settled, and from here on he collects rooms of that kind the way other men collect land. The Observatory sits south of the river with the meridian cut through its floor, and the men who work in it answer to the Bureau.

stops.name: Institut de France, the brackets of 1809
stops.date_confidence: attested by Y. Kosmann-Schwarzbach, SIGMA 18 (2022) 092, p.11, that the bracket expression appears in Poisson's 1809 memoir on the variation of arbitrary constants, that it was called simply an expression for a century, that one author in 1872 wrote of 'Poisson's notation', and that the name Poisson brackets was standardised only with E. T. Whittaker's history of 1910. Month not recorded. The closing sentence reaches past Poisson's death to 1925 and to a subject with his own file in this corpus; that reach is flagged for the operator in the report and is not licensed by EXCEPTIONS.md, on which Poisson is not listed. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from evariste_galois.journey.json.
stops.campa: In a memoir on the variation of arbitrary constants he writes down a combination of derivatives that measures how two quantities of a mechanical system fail to leave each other alone. He gives it no name. For a hundred years it is called an expression, or Poisson's notation, and Whittaker's history of 1910 is what finally fixes the name to him. In 1925 Dirac, out walking near Cambridge on a Sunday with every library shut, remembers the shape of it and cannot check until Monday whether quantum quantities obey the same algebra. They do.
suggested_refs: Poisson, memoir on the variation of arbitrary constants (1809)

stops.name: The Sorbonne, professor of rational mechanics
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and fr.wikipedia: appointed professor of rational mechanics in the newly organised Faculté des sciences de Paris in 1809. Month not recorded. The Faculté was housed at the Sorbonne; the coordinate is corrected from the research pool's 48.8469, 2.3444, which falls about 250 m south of the block, to 48.8487, 2.3437, close to the Nominatim position for the Sorbonne at 48.8494, 2.3445. The saying quoted is [R]: attributed to Poisson through Arago and quoted by fr.wikipedia and MacTutor, but no instance of it was traced to the text of Arago's eulogy itself.
stops.campa: The university is rebuilt under the Empire and Poisson is given rational mechanics in the new Faculté des sciences. He now holds the Polytechnique chair, this one, and the Bureau, and he keeps all three at once. Teaching is not a duty he endures in order to be left alone with his research. It is half of what he says a life is for. At twenty-eight he is lecturing in three institutions to boys who will run the bridges, the artillery and the schools of France, and he is doing his own work in the hours between. The saying comes down through Arago, who heard him say it, and has never been found written in Poisson's own hand.
stops.quote: La vie n'est bonne qu'à deux choses : à faire des mathématiques et à les professer.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Poisson by François Arago; quoted in fr.wikipedia, 'Siméon Denis Poisson', and in English translation in the MacTutor biography. Not located in the text of Arago's eulogy.

stops.name: École Polytechnique, the Traité de mécanique
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor for the 1811 publication of the Traité de mécanique in two volumes. Month not recorded. The Libri passage is [R]: attributed to G. Libri's contemporary notice of Poisson and seen only in the MacTutor compilation, not traced to Libri's original French. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json.
stops.campa: The two volumes of the Traité de mécanique come out of ten years of lecturing and become the book the school teaches from. It is not a book of discoveries. It is an ordering: what mechanics consists of, in what sequence, in what notation, for a generation of men who will lay out the roads and cast the guns. He works on one thing at a time. Whatever else occurs to him while he is working goes into a notebook in his pocket and waits, sometimes for years, until its turn comes.
stops.quote: Poisson never wished to occupy himself with two things at the same time; when, in the course of his labours, a research project crossed his mind that did not form any immediate connection with what he was doing at the time, he contented himself with writing a few words in his little wallet...
stops.quote_source: Attributed to G. Libri's contemporary notice of Poisson, quoted in translation in the MacTutor biography

stops.name: Institut de France, elected at thirty
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1812 by MacTutor and en.wikipedia: elected to the physics section of the Institut de France after an earlier unsuccessful candidacy. No month is recorded, so the order of this stop against the memoir of 9 March 1812 is not established and the January date is an ordering device only. stops.campa: He is elected to the physics section of the Institute at thirty, having stood once before and lost. From this date he is not only a producer of French science but one of the men who decide what French science is: referee, examiner, reporter, the reader whose word can end a paper before it is printed. He sits under Mazarin's dome on the quai de Conti for twenty-eight years and misses very little. His work since Arcueil has been electricity, heat and capillarity done with Laplace's analysis. Why the physics section and not the mathematics one, nothing reached says.

stops.name: Institut de France, electricity on the surface of bodies
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor for the submission to the Academy on 9 March 1812 of the solution on the distribution of electricity on the surfaces of conducting bodies. That the extension of Laplace's potential theory to regions containing source density is the origin of what is now written as the Poisson equation is a synthesis of the research pool and standard accounts, and is not stated in those words by the sources reached. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from evariste_galois.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the ninth of March he lays before the Academy a solution for the way electric charge distributes itself over the surface of a conductor. The mathematics takes Laplace's equation for the potential, which holds where there is nothing, and rewrites it for the places where there is something: a source density on the right-hand side where Laplace had a zero. It is one term of difference. He puts it forward to settle a question about charged metal, and says nothing about what else that equation might be made to carry.
suggested_refs: Poisson's memoirs on the distribution of electricity, 1811-1813, Mémoires de la classe des sciences
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), biography of Siméon-Denis Poisson

stops.name: Institut de France, Fourier's complaint to Laplace
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The 1815 complaint by Fourier to Laplace, that Poisson and Biot had added no result different from his own while claiming a better exposition, comes through the research dossier and is corroborated in outline by the well documented Fourier-Poisson priority dispute in histories of the Academy; the letter itself was not opened in this pass. Month not recorded. The Fourier quotation is [R]: seen only in the MacTutor compilation, with the original French document not located. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from evariste_galois.journey.json.
stops.campa: Seven years after the summary signed P, Fourier writes to Laplace that Poisson and Biot have found nothing he had not already found and are claiming only to have said it better. The quarrel does not resolve. It goes on in memoirs, in referees' reports, in the temperature of committee minutes, until one of the two men is dead. Later historians give Fourier the theory and the series, and allow that several of Poisson's technical objections were fair. Fourier's own verdict on him is one sentence long.
stops.quote: Poisson has too much talent to apply it to the work of others. To use it to discover what is already known is to waste it...
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Joseph Fourier on Poisson, quoted in translation in the MacTutor biography of Poisson

stops.name: Saint-Cyr-l'École, examiner for the École Militaire
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor: examiner for the École Militaire in 1815, listed separately from the École Polytechnique examinership of 1816. The research pool recorded an unresolved 1815 versus 1816 contradiction here; it is not a contradiction but two different posts, and that flag is dropped. No month recorded. No lens supplied a coordinate for this stop: 48.7996, 2.0656 is the commune of Saint-Cyr-l'École, taken from general geography rather than an opened gazetteer, and marks the town, not a building.
stops.campa: The military school takes him on as an examiner. It is the year of Waterloo, the second Restoration and the purges, and what he is doing in it is going out to Saint-Cyr to decide which boys are fit to be artillery officers. The regime that appointed him has fallen; the regime that replaces it keeps him on, because the boys still have to be graded and nobody else can grade them. He will hold examining posts of one kind or another until the week he dies. The two schools are separate appointments, made a year apart, and the biographies that report a single post moved from one year to the other have collapsed two jobs into one.

stops.name: École Polytechnique, the examiner at the exit
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia for 1816: examiner of the final examinations at the École Polytechnique in place of Lacroix, a post held until his death. Month not recorded. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from augustin_louis_cauchy.journey.json.
stops.campa: He takes Lacroix's place as the man who examines the leaving class. Every graduate of the school for the next twenty-four years passes in front of him, and the rank he assigns settles which corps a boy enters and therefore what his life will be. The professorship the reorganisation cost him is worth less than this. Nobody who describes him says he built a faction with it; what they say is that he asked questions and marked the answers. He holds the post until he dies, still examining in the spring of 1840.

That is the whole of what the record holds. No letters between them, no description of the household, no anecdote that is not about mathematics, not even a firm list of the children's names. A man whose working day is documented hour by hour across forty years leaves a marriage of twenty-three years almost entirely unwitnessed.

stops.name: Somerset House, London: a fellow who never crossed
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and en.wikipedia, the latter dating the election to March 1818; no day given. [R] as to place: no evidence was found that Poisson ever travelled to England, and election as a foreign member is conferred in absentia, so the coordinate marks the Royal Society's premises at Somerset House, its home from 1780 to 1857, rather than any ground he stood on.
stops.campa: The Royal Society elects him a fellow in March. He does not come to London. Foreign members are elected in their absence and stay where they are, and the diploma travels to Paris while he goes on with his week. The Society is quartered at Somerset House on the Strand, and its rooms will never hold him. He is thirty-six, and this is the first of the foreign honours; they go on arriving for the rest of his life, from Edinburgh, from Boston, from Stockholm.

stops.name: Institut de France, the absurd bright spot
stops.date_confidence: attested by MacTutor and by en.wikipedia's 'Arago spot' that Poisson sat on the Academy's diffraction prize commission with Laplace, Biot and Arago, and that from Fresnel's equations he deduced a bright point at the centre of the shadow of a small opaque disk. Entries for the competition were due on 1 August 1818, which is the date used here to order the stop; the deduction itself is not dated to a day in any source reached. The theatrical version in which Poisson declares the result impossible and is publicly humiliated is a later narrative of wave optics and is not carried as fact. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from evariste_galois.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Academy has set a prize on diffraction and Augustin Fresnel has entered a memoir arguing that light is a wave. Poisson, who holds with the corpuscles, works through Fresnel's own equations to see what they commit a man to, and finds this: put a small round disk in a beam of light and there will be a bright point at the exact centre of its shadow, where the disk is thickest. He submits the result to the commission as a refutation. The algebra is correct.
suggested_refs: Fresnel's prize memoir on diffraction, Académie des sciences competition of 1817-1819
sources: MacTutor (St Andrews), account of the Academy diffraction competition

stops.name: Institut de France, the disk on the glass plate
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia ('Arago spot') that Arago tested the deduction with a small metal disk and observed the spot, that Fresnel was awarded the prize in 1819, and that the spot had been seen by Delisle in 1715 and Maraldi in 1723. The research pool dated the experiment itself to March 1819; that is not supported, the competition timeline places the experiment in the commission's deliberations of late 1818, and March 1819 belongs to the award. The date here is the award, and the campa places the experiment before it. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from evariste_galois.journey.json.
stops.campa: Arago mounts a metal disk two millimetres across on a glass plate, puts it in the beam and looks into the middle of the shadow, where the calculation says the light cannot get. The point of light is there. The commission gives Fresnel the prize in 1819, Poisson signing the award with the rest, and the corpuscular account of light begins a retreat it does not come back from. The spot is named for Poisson. Delisle had seen it in 1715 and Maraldi in 1723, and neither of them could say what it was.

Delisle (1715) and Maraldi (1723), earlier observations of the spot

stops.name: Institut de France, the ratio

stops.campa: Pull a wire and it gets longer and it gets thinner. Measurement broke the universality within a decade and kept the ratio, which runs differently in every substance. In 1987 Roderic Lakes built a foam whose ratio is negative.
